ratings.reason: A strong match: revision labels fork into alternatives, and confirming one selection commits it to further refinement. The quote does not specify the gallery’s layout or number of alternatives, so it falls short of a definitive exemplar.

Three generated documentation options appear together in a dropdown, which strongly implies selection of one downstream. This is highly transferable and rebuildable, though conventional and the quote does not explicitly state the commit behavior.

The system visibly presents three same-type phrase suggestions as separate list items. The title and framing make choice central, but the supplied quote does not explicitly describe selecting one and discarding the others.

A textbook candidate gallery: four simultaneous renderings, one selected as the best match, with regeneration as an optional reset. The mechanism is concrete and portable, although the basic interaction is not especially novel.

The quote gives the complete core sequence: generate four images, display them, then select one. It is exceptionally clear and transferable, but essentially the default image-generation gallery pattern.

Users choose among generated prompt suggestions, after which the selected candidate alone is rephrased into the editable downstream prompt. The transformation after selection makes this a particularly useful and transferable implementation variant.

A list of generated questions supplies alternatives, and selecting one commits it as the filter controlling the article view. This clearly shows choice affecting downstream state, though the quote does not specify how many questions appear.

Simultaneous execution results for multiple code variations clearly establish the gallery half of the pattern and make alternatives unusually concrete. The evidence never says that selecting one commits it downstream or terminates the other branches.

VISAR presents generated aspects for selection, but users may select multiple aspects to explore rather than resolve the set by committing one candidate. It is closer to multi-select scope construction than the pattern’s one-of-N commit.

The evidence establishes that four ranked viewpoints are shown, but not that the user chooses one or that a choice changes downstream state. On the supplied evidence it is a ranked comparison display, not a complete candidate-gallery interaction.

Multiple renderings are displayed together, but users freely arrange them on a persistent palette rather than resolve the set through a single commit. This sits nearer an exploratory alternative workspace than Candidate Gallery.

The interaction is fully specified: the first agent proposes four same-type purposes, the user selects one, and that choice triggers the next agent. It cleanly demonstrates selection as a downstream commit and is easy to reuse in other staged workflows.

Multiple candidate inputs are explicitly presented for user selection, making the pattern central to the interface variation. The abstract-level quote omits the number, visual arrangement, and precise downstream effect, limiting rebuildability.

Generating three potential next steps is a plausible candidate gallery that materially steers a plan. However, the quote does not explicitly say they are shown together, that the programmer selects one, or how selection commits the plan.

The widget exposes same-type reply candidates with deliberate sentiment coverage, but only two of the six are visible at once and selection is not stated. It partially matches the structural signature while introducing pagination or cycling within the set.

The agent offers three contextually plausible answers together and the participant chooses among them. It is a clean, highly transferable candidate gallery whose uncertainty-management use is more interesting than a generic generation picker.

Showing model-considered alternatives at an exact decoding decision point is a distinctive and potentially powerful fork. The supplied quote does not establish that the user selects one or explain how the selected alternative changes generated code, so the core commit remains underspecified.

The system generates three related characters, but the evidence does not say they are alternatives shown together or that the writer selects exactly one. All three may simply be additions to the ensemble, which would violate the one-of-N resolution requirement.

Participants receive three suggestions and can choose one or regenerate, closely matching the gallery-and-resolution flow. The quote leaves the visual arrangement and downstream commitment implicit, so it is strong rather than definitive evidence.

Preference is expressed by repeatedly choosing among generated results, and each choice guides subsequent optimization. This makes Candidate Gallery the control mechanism, although the quote does not explicitly confirm simultaneous display and the iterative loop extends beyond a single resolution act.

SPROUT presents three ranked choices with a useful visual encoding of voting strength, but the evidence does not show a user selection or downstream commit. The candidates may be agent-voting results rather than alternatives resolved by the user.

Curating from diversity-aware recommendations suggests some alternative selection, but the quote supplies no candidate count, joint presentation, one-of-N choice, or commit behavior. Impact and novelty cannot be judged confidently from the title and this evidence alone.

Users select among diverse generated suggestions through gaze, making candidate choice the operative control. The interaction is clear and distinctive, but the quote omits the number and layout, while reliance on AR gaze hardware reduces direct transferability.

Each turn visibly supplies three same-type response options, a highly reusable branching-choice structure. User selection and the resulting next scene are strongly implied by “response options” but not explicitly stated in the supplied quote.

Six direction clusters are simultaneously displayed using representative images, giving designers a concrete comparative gallery. The evidence does not state that selecting one commits a direction or backgrounds the others, so only the presentation half is firmly supported.

The quote only establishes that the prototype provides generative image suggestions. It does not demonstrate multiple options shown together, user selection, or downstream commitment; accessibility impact is plausible from the title but cannot be assessed strongly from the available evidence.

Children select multiple generated keywords that are combined to produce two storylines. This is multi-select input composition, not a one-of-N choice among same-type outputs where unchosen branches terminate.

Two candidate voices are evaluated and one preference is recorded, clearly capturing comparative selection. The evidence does not show simultaneous rendering in a bounded gallery or explain whether the preferred voice is committed into the communication aid.

The pipeline generates candidate contextual questions, presents them as choices, and uses the selected question to launch a downstream visualization. It clearly specifies both the selection action and resulting state change and transfers readily beyond statistical reading.

Three same-type dance sequences are generated from one description and displayed together as thumbnails, strongly demonstrating the gallery. The quote does not show selection or commitment, so the defining resolution half of the pattern remains unsupported.
